next.name: GOLD LOCUST
next.headline: GOLD LOCUST: a long-tracked group known as FIN7 and Carbanak, with loaders and ransomware ties
next.in_short: Secureworks tracks GOLD LOCUST and lists FIN7 and Carbanak among its aliases. Researchers describe its malware loaders and tie it to ransomware-linked intrusions. Several of these links are assessments, not settled fact.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as GOLD LOCUST. Its catalogue record lists the aliases Anunak, Carbanak, Carbon Spider, FIN7 and Silicon.
The same record lists Carbanak as a tool linked to the group.
Malwarebytes Threat Intelligence attributes a late-June malspam campaign to FIN7, a name the catalogue lists as an alias. The emails dropped a loader called JSSLoader.
Malwarebytes describes JSSLoader as a rewrite with expanded capabilities, including data exfiltration. It also dropped a secondary payload written in .NET.
The same report notes an earlier component of FIN7 that others had described. It was delivered in the XLL file format.

SentinelLABS published a report on 3 November 2022 about Black Basta ransomware attacks. It says the custom EDR evasion tools used in them are tied to FIN7. The title describes a link, not a flat identity.
Rapid7 cites GData, which attributes a Python RAT it calls Anubis to FIN7.
In a 2020 ransomware overview, IBM Security X-Force reports investigating a Carbanak backdoor associated with a Sodinokibi ransomware attack.
IBM assesses that a group it calls ITG14 is at least one affiliate group that contracts with Sodinokibi providers. The report says the Carbanak link rests on similarity to ITG14 tools.
Rapid7 assesses that the developers of a Java malware family are likely initial access brokers. It says they potentially provided access for Black Basta and/or FIN7 affiliates.
Treat unexpected loaders and unfamiliar remote-access sessions as signs of possible hands-on intrusion, and investigate them quickly.
